claims.text: His own identification and background, on his site's about page: he is Tom Mahood, he worked as a civil engineer and traffic engineer for Orange County, California, later City Traffic Engineer for Orange, and he holds a Master's degree in physics from Cal State Fullerton.

His conclusion on the credentials: 'Lazar never attended either CalTech or MIT. Of this I am certain of beyond a reasonable doubt.' His investigation records that 'Standard inquiries have been made by George Knapp and Stanton Friedman and turned up nothing'; that Glenn Campbell in 1993 found no Lazar 'in any MIT student directory between 1978 and 1990'; and that Natalie Gilmore of Caltech Graduate Studies stated that Caltech 'does not currently have, nor has it ever had any sort of graduate degree in electronics or electronic technology'.

claims.source: Tom Mahood, 'Looking at the Bob Lazar story from the perspective of 2018', https://otherhand.org/home-page/area-51-and-other-strange-places/looking-at-the-bob-lazar-story-from-the-perspective-of-2018/ , opened 2026-09-18
claims.text: His 2018 retrospective concludes that there is 'nothing at Papoose Lake', that S-4 actually refers to a radar facility at the Tonopah Test Range, and that Lazar constructed the alien-craft narrative as a cover after security caught him bringing friends to watch classified tests in April 1989. It concedes in the same document that Lazar is 'amazingly believable', that Mahood initially found the story plausible before investigating the details, and that Lazar demonstrated real technical cleverness as a troubleshooter.

On the Los Alamos question he concludes that Lazar worked as an electronic technician for the contractor Kirk-Mayer rather than as a staff physicist, that the phone-directory listing reflects that contractor relationship, and that the Monitor article's description followed what Lazar told the reporter. He also accepts that the W-2 could be legitimate, representing a brief stint at Groom, while insisting 'it doesn't mean saucers exist at Papoose'.

On element 115 his page assembles the prior art: Glenn Seaborg's article in Scientific American of April 1969, pages 57 to 67, with graphics of expected half-lives for superheavy elements, and a 1970 textbook describing element 114, with 114 protons and 184 neutrons, as 'an island of stability in a sea of instability'. The island of stability was published popular physics long before 1989.

label: Tom Mahood
narrative: Tom Mahood is the custody and analysis point for most of the documentary record in this cluster, and without a node for him the board's case-against edges have nothing to originate from. He describes himself on his own site as a former civil engineer and traffic engineer for Orange County, California, with a Master's degree in physics from Cal State Fullerton. His otherhand.org investigation reprints the Los Alamos Monitor front page of 27 June 1982, both Las Vegas Review-Journal reports of 1990, Mark Farmer's 1996 taped interview with an anonymised Los Alamos colleague, and David L. Morgan's physics critique, and it quotes Lazar's 1990 Pre-Sentence Report. His conclusion on the credentials is flat: 'Lazar never attended either CalTech or MIT. Of this I am certain of beyond a reasonable doubt.' His 2018 retrospective is the single best case-against document in the cluster precisely because it concedes what is true, granting that Lazar is 'amazingly believable', that Mahood himself initially found the story plausible, and that Lazar showed genuine technical cleverness. His counter-explanation is that there is nothing at Papoose Lake, that S-4 is a designator attaching to a Tonopah Test Range radar facility, and that the account began as a cover story after security caught Lazar bringing friends to watch classified tests in April 1989.
